sources.entry: Part 1: Integers, Lexing and Code Generation

summary.title: Writing a C Compiler, Part 1
summary.one_liner: You learn how to build the first stage of a C compiler by lexing, parsing into an AST, and generating x86 assembly for a program that returns an integer.
takeaways: A compiler can be split into lexing, parsing into an AST, and code generation, each a small testable step.
Recursive descent parsing turns a token list into an AST by writing one function per grammar non-terminal.
A minimal program returning a constant compiles to a few x86 instructions: movl into %eax, then ret.
Using a language with sum types and pattern matching (OCaml, Haskell, Rust) makes AST handling easier.
The series targets 32-bit x86 (following Ghuloum's paper); 64-bit adaptation is left to the reader for now.
summary.summary: This is the first part of a series on writing a C compiler, adapted from Abdulaziz Ghuloum's incremental compiler paper. It covers the reasons to build a compiler, language and parser choices, and a week-one target: compiling a C program that returns a single decimal integer. The post walks through lexing (with token regexes), defining AST nodes and a BNF grammar, recursive descent parsing, and emitting AT&T x86 assembly, with gcc output used as a reference. It ends with a driver that invokes gcc -m32 and a reference to a test script; the author notes the series uses 32-bit output and that 64-bit examples were planned.
